title: Ang 585–594: Vadhans ki Var
tomorrow: what seed would Guru Nanak plant in the field of a body?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dirges: songs for the dead that open with blessed is the Creator. Don't call death bad, if you know how to die. Now Vadhans closes with a ballad.

Every feed has its copies: the same outfit, the same morning routine, the same candid-looking pose that took ages to get right. Guru Ram Das's ballad in Vadhans begins on ang 585, and among the saloks set beside it is a picture of exactly that. The herons watched the swans gliding on the water and wanted to swim too. They waded in, and drowned: heads down, feet in the air.
screen: `EVERY FEED HAS ITS COPIES.` → `THE HERONS WATCH THE SWANS.` → `HEADS DOWN, FEET UP.`

segments.voice: A var is a ballad: stanzas called pauris, here by Guru Ram Das, with short saloks set beside them, many by Guru Amar Das. In this one, in paraphrase, the swans are those steeped in the Word, holding the true Name in the heart. The herons see them and copy the swimming. Sikh readers take this salok more than one way. Some hear a warning against show. Their best case: the herons copied what swans do, not what makes them swans, and the copy is what sank them. A practice worn on the outside for others to see goes under. Others hear a door left open. Their best case: the salok defines a swan by the Word and the Name, not by birth, and the Word is what the Guru gives. So the lesson isn't stay on the bank; it's that swimming comes from the inside, and the inside can be received. Both readings agree the herons' mistake was copying the surface. They differ on what the ballad most wants you to hear: a caution, or an invitation. Both are said by people who love the same page. That's the fourth's ballad, and Vadhans ends here.
screen: `A VAR: PAURIS, WITH SALOKS.` · `SWANS: STEEPED IN THE WORD.` · `ONE READING: A WARNING AGAINST SHOW.` · `ANOTHER: THE INSIDE CAN BE RECEIVED.` · then, large: `THE FOURTH'S BALLAD.`

segments.voice: Say the two readings out loud, slowly, one after the other: the herons copied the surface; the inside can be received. Then sit with whichever one you resisted, and say its best case once more in your own words. Let the rest of the sit be quiet.
Ang 585. Where Vadhans ki Var begins: Guru Ram Das's ballad, with saloks of swans and herons beside it.
Pocket this one: the fourth's ballad, where the swimming comes from the inside. Vadhans, finished and closed.

howItsDone: Vars in the Guru Granth Sahib are read and sung in the sangat like other hymns; each pauri comes with saloks placed beside it, and the reader moves through them in order.
